newsitem.title: USA: Texas Instruments reports loss but stock soars.
newsitem.headline: Texas Instruments reports loss but stock soars.

text.p: Texas Instruments Inc. reported a fourth-quarter loss Thursday, but its stock soared about 14 percent as investors looked beyond the bottom line and saw a firm recovery in its core semiconductor business.
The Dallas-based semiconductor giant posted a loss of $29 million, or 15 cents per share, compared with a profit of $291 million, or $1.50 per share, in the fourth quarter of 1995.
Revenues fell to $2.46 billion from $3.15 billion, primarily because of a huge drop in the price of computer memory chips..

The results were depressed by one-time charges. Company executives said operating profits were 67 cents a share, roughly in line with analyst expectations. Operating profits were more than double those of the third quarter.
Texas Instruments also announced it was selling its notebook computer business to Taiwan-based Acer Inc..

While the terms of the deal were not disclosed, analysts welcomed the move, and the company's stock jumped $10 to $73.50 on the New York Stock Exchange in afternoon trading, making it one of the biggest percentage gainers on the exchange.

Texas Instruments earlier this month sold its defense electronics unit to Raytheon Co. for $2.95 billion, and the sale of the notebook computer unit fits in with the company's plan to focus its efforts on higher-margin digital signal processors, or DSPS, which convert sights and sounds into digital computer language.

"We are accelerating our strategic direction by focusing on businesses, products and technologies that add value for TI and our customers through sustainable differentiation, with high-growth opportunities and improved financial stability," Chief Executive Officer Tom Engibous said. "1997 will be a year of transition."
Analysts said the rapid shift away from low-growth businesses to digital signal processors was transforming Texas Instruments' profile and would boost profits.

"They are becoming an entirely different company. You are not going to recognize them at all in '97," said Daniel Niles, an analyst with brokerage Robertson Stephens. "They are blowing out of the unprofitable PC business and are left with the high-growth semiconductor business."
Niles said he expected Texas Instruments' share price to double over the next 12 to 18 months.

Chief Financial Officer Bill Aylesworth said the troubled market for memory chips would remain volatile in the short term because of excess supply but that new chip products were taking up much of the slack.
Memory chip prices fell about 80 percent last year and dragged down Texas Instrument's yearly net profits to $63 million, or 33 cents a share, from $1.09 billion, or $5.63 a share, in 1995.

Orders for digital signal processors, however, were 30 percent higher in the fourth quarter, and Aylseworth predicted strong growth in 1997. "We see every indication that the trend of strong revenue growth is going to continue," he said in an interview.

Aylesworth said one-time special charges in the fourth quarter included $91 million in severance costs related to a voluntary retirement plan and $117 million in asset write-downs on certain product lines in the notebook computer unit as well as a $15 million additional tax provision.
